headline: Ram Island bait pinned tight to the rocks: albies through the Race, bass starting to stage
subhead: The boulder fields from Wamphassuc to Fishers Island are holding peanut bunker against structure, and the albie run finally reached our water this week.
body_markdown:
Peanut bunker and silversides have been pinning themselves against the granite all week — tight against the boulder fields off Ram Island, stacked in the current seams at Wamphassuc Point, balled up along the Esker Point rocks on the last of the ebb. That's the tell. When bait gets nervous and glues itself to structure instead of running open water, something's pushing it, and this week it was albies working the edges of Fishers Island Sound and current pouring through the Race.

We flagged this on the 7th — said the Race would be a top pick for the albie run as fish pushed through on the strong tides, and that's exactly what happened. The run that blew up off Rhode Island in early September kept its momentum and spread west right into our water. Fish are showing at the Race itself, off the west end of Fishers Island, and working the rip lines off Wilderness Point on the moving tide. Bonito are mixed in but outnumbered — most of what's coming to the boat right now is albies, and the sizes have been decent, not giant, but plenty of them in the right window.

The thermal setup explains why the push is holding here instead of sliding past. New London is reading 69.4 and Kings Point out west is a touch warmer at 70.9 — that gradient is keeping bait concentrated rather than scattered, and albies don't chase scattered bait, they chase panic. The panic has been happening in short, violent windows — the last hour of the ebb into dead low, and the first hour of the flood, right when the current is ripping hardest through the Race and around the reefs off the west end. Outside those windows the water goes quiet and the fish disappear for a while, so timing matters more than location right now.

On the boat, small profile metal has been the call — half-ounce and three-quarter-ounce Deadly Dicks, epoxy jigs, and Albie Snax in bone or pink-white, cast into the boils and worked back fast with no pause. Fly guys have been doing just as well or better in the tighter pushes, throwing half-and-half patterns and small Clouser-style baitfish on intermediate lines, letting the fly swing through the seam rather than stripping it against the grain of the current. The fish have been fussy about retrieve speed on bright days and considerably less picky under cloud cover or in low light, so early mornings before the sun gets high have been the more forgiving window.

Striped bass are still mostly a rocks-and-shadows story rather than a blitz story. Bunker schools have started tightening up in the back corners of Little Narragansett Bay and around the mouth of the Mystic River, and there's early interest from bass shadowing them tight to structure rather than committing hard yet. This lines up with what's happening from Raritan Bay on up — the fall bunker exodus is underway, and the fish are just beginning to show real intent instead of picking at stragglers. The better bass have been coming off the boulder fields on the outgoing tide, drifted with 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with a strip of fluke belly, worked slow along bottom where the rock drops into deeper water off Ram Island and the outer edge of the Stonington breakwater. Nothing has been easy — it's a fish here, a fish there, not a pattern you can set a watch to yet — but the pieces are lining up the way they do in mid-September before things tighten in October.

Blackfish season isn't quite in gear yet up here — a few feeder tog have shown on the deeper rockpiles off Wamphassuc and around the breakwater rubble, but nothing worth planning a trip around. That bite typically doesn't get serious in this zone until the water eases further and the crabs and green crab pieces start drawing real numbers, so hold that thought for later in the month.

Fluke have been thinning out of the shallow flats in Little Narragansett Bay as the water cools, sliding toward the deeper channel edges near Watch Hill and the mouth of the Pawcatuck. A few keepers are still coming on Gulp Swimming Mullets in white, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the ebb, but this bite is fading fast and won't hold much longer as those fish continue their push toward deeper water.

The next few days look like more of the same setup, maybe better. Tides are building toward the next push, which should keep bait pinned against the rocks and keep the albie windows tight but productive around the Race and the west end of Fishers Island. If the wind stays out of the north or west and lays down in the mornings, the dawn window at the Race and off Wilderness Point is the one worth building a morning around — clean water, hard current, and fish that have shown they'll commit when the bait gets squeezed. Keep an eye on the bass pattern too. If bunker keep tightening in the back bays the way they have from here down through Narragansett Bay, the next real move should be bass committing harder to structure on the outgoing tide rather than just shadowing bait from a distance. That shift usually comes fast once it starts.
